_meta.purpose: Real-world precedent for grounding EVAL01 scenario parameters (config/benchmark/panama.yaml + scenario YAMLs, once written) for the Panama Canal chokepoint, matching the structure and honesty conventions of data/routing_research/hormuz_rerouting_patterns.json.
_meta.labeling: Each numeric value carries an evidence tag: 'documented' (a cited source states the number) or 'extrapolated' (derived/interpolated — the derivation is recorded in that event's 'notes'). A null value is a correct result when no credible source was found; it is explained, not guessed.
_meta.key_finding: Panama's primary documented disruption driver (2023-2024) is HYDROLOGICAL and SLOW-ONSET — a multi-month drought that gradually tightened a daily transit-slot cap, not a sudden geopolitical or physical-blockage event. This is structurally distinct from every other chokepoint in this benchmark (Hormuz/Bab el-Mandeb = geopolitical/security; Suez 2021 = instantaneous physical blockage) and is precisely why Panama belongs in this benchmark: it exercises the pipeline's ability to detect a slowly-ramping capacity constraint with weeks of lead time, not a step-function shock. A second, structurally OPPOSITE 2026 event is also documented below: a demand-side surge (not a supply-side restriction) caused by spillover from the Hormuz closure, which strained an already-near-capacity canal from the other direction.
_meta.units_convention: Per docs/multiregion/BENCHMARK_SCHEMA_REFERENCE.md: the EVAL01 pipeline's 'shipping' signal is a raw vessel-transit count/day; 'market' is an unbounded, roughly z-score-like index; 'geopolitical'/'routing'/'news'/'disaster' are 0-1 normalized scores. Values below are recorded in their real-world documented units; mapping to the pipeline's internal convention is scenario-authoring work for a later prompt.

events.name: 2023-2024 Gatun Lake drought and transit-slot restrictions

shipping.unit: vessels/day (transit-slot cap) and total annual transits (FY = Oct-Sep)

geopolitical.explanation: No geopolitical driver applies — this event is purely hydrological/climate-driven (El Nino-linked rainfall deficit). See key_finding above.

disaster.unit: Gatun Lake elevation in feet above sea level; permitted vessel draft in feet

value.maersk_land_bridge_intermodal_diversion: OC1 service dropped its Cartagena port call and used Balboa rail transit to Manzanillo to catch Philadelphia/Charleston sailings, Jan-May 2024

routing.unit: days (queue wait time, no-reservation vessels); vessels/day (Neopanamax locks); vessel count (Stolt-Nielsen fleet diverted); % (rail-diversion share of diverted cargo); days (Magellan Strait detour)
routing.explanation: A follow-up targeted search (2026-08-12, A4.5-equivalent pass) specifically for DIVERSION (not congestion) evidence found it: Stolt-Nielsen (166-vessel chemical-tanker fleet) publicly announced in Nov 2023 it was rerouting via the Suez Canal because Panama service had become 'increasingly unreliable,' charging customers for the longer route (TradeWinds/Bloomberg/AJOT, corroborating). Maersk separately used a Balboa-Manzanillo rail 'land bridge' to bypass the canal for part of its OC1 service. These are genuine route DEVIATION (vessels not transiting Panama at all), structurally distinct from the wait-time/queueing figures above (vessels still transiting, just slower) — see this event's notes for why both are recorded and why neither alone is 'the' routing signal for this region.

news.explanation: No news-sentiment/volume index specific to this event was located. The month-by-month transit-cap tightening schedule (shipping field above) is a plausible proxy for the shape of a slow-building news-coverage ramp — climate/drought stories accumulate coverage as restrictions visibly worsen — but this is not itself a measured signal.

events.notes: Sources vary slightly (32-38 vessels/day) on the exact starting daily-transit figure and the exact per-step cap at each date, likely reflecting different sources counting Panamax-only vs. combined Panamax+Neopanamax locks, and slightly different snapshot dates within the same month. The ranges recorded above reflect that spread rather than picking one source arbitrarily; treat the general shape (36-38 -> ~32 -> ~28-30 -> 22-24 -> recovery) as the documented finding, and any single-day exact figure as approximate. Recovery was gradual, not a step function: restrictions eased starting 2024-01-16 and capacity was not fully restored to ~36/day until August 2024 — roughly 7 months of graduated recovery following ~4 months of tightening, i.e. the recovery tail is longer than the onset ramp, unlike a typical geopolitical-event decay curve. CONGESTION VS. DIVERSION (resolved 2026-08-12): the routing field mixes two structurally different signals on purpose. Wait-time/Neopanamax-transit figures measure congestion AT the canal (vessels still transiting, just slower) — a route-deviation model over AIS data (this codebase's routing_connector.py/routing_agent) cannot detect that on its own, since the vessel's path doesn't change. The Stolt-Nielsen/Maersk figures measure genuine diversion AWAY from the canal (vessels take a different physical path entirely) — this IS what a route-deviation model can detect. Both are real and documented; neither should be presented as the whole picture. Diversion appears to be a minority behavior relative to the much larger population that queued or paid auction premiums instead (no source found gives a total-fleet diversion percentage), so treat the routing signal as real but modest in scale, not dominant.

events.name: 2026 Hormuz-crisis demand surge and capacity strain

shipping.value: operating close to maximum daily capacity (~36-40 transits/day)

geopolitical.value: surge driven by Asian buyers seeking non-Middle-East-Gulf energy supply routes following the 2026-02-28+ Strait of Hormuz closure

disaster.explanation: Not applicable — this event's driver is a demand shift, not a hazard.

news.explanation: No dedicated sentiment/volume index found; not derived here.

events.notes: STRUCTURALLY OPPOSITE to the 2023-2024 drought event: this is a demand-side surge (more vessels wanting to transit, competing for a capacity that is fundamentally intact) rather than a supply-side restriction (fewer transits permitted due to water scarcity). Auction prices spike in both events, but for opposite underlying reasons — worth flagging if a scenario author is tempted to treat 'high auction price' as a single undifferentiated signal; the shipping/routing signal shapes differ (drought: falling daily-transit count; 2026 surge: transit count near its ceiling, wait time rising instead). This event is also cross-linked to the SAME 2026-02-28 Hormuz closure documented in data/routing_research/hormuz_rerouting_patterns.json and in data/region_research/bab_el_mandeb_disruption_patterns.json's second event — three chokepoints (Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb, Panama) all show a documented response to the identical trigger date, though the sign and mechanism of Panama's response (demand surge, capacity strain) is opposite to Bab el-Mandeb's (traffic collapse, avoidance). A scheduled Panama lock-maintenance window (March-September 2026) overlaps this event and independently tightens capacity — the two effects are not cleanly separable in the sources found here (see limitations).

limitations: (1) No credible source describes a full CLOSURE of the Panama Canal in either documented event — the canal has never stopped operating; only the daily-transit cap and wait times moved. This is a structural fact worth preserving explicitly: Panama's disruption ceiling is 'severely constrained, still open' (~40-50% of a normal-year total in the worst FY), never 'closed' the way Hormuz was in 2026 or Suez was during the six-day Ever Given grounding. (2) The 2026 event's numbers are entangled with a separately-documented, concurrent scheduled lock-maintenance window (March-September 2026); sources found in this pass did not cleanly separate how much of the wait-time/price increase is maintenance-driven vs. Hormuz-demand-driven, so treat the 2026 event's magnitude as an upper-bound combined effect, not a pure Hormuz-attributable figure. (3) No 'news' sentiment/volume index was found for either event; both news fields are marked extrapolated and left without a proxy value (only a qualitative note on what a proxy might look like). (4) A specific market-domain figure independent of auction-slot price (e.g. a freight-rate or trade-value-at-risk figure specific to Panama-transiting cargo) was not located in this pass. (5) CONGESTION VS. DIVERSION (originally an open ambiguity in this file; resolved 2026-08-12 by a targeted follow-up search): an earlier version of this file's 2023-2024 event routing field contained only queueing/wait-time figures, which measure congestion AT the canal, not diversion AWAY from it — a route-deviation model (this codebase's routing_connector.py/routing_agent) cannot detect congestion on its own, since a queued vessel's path hasn't changed. The follow-up search specifically for diversion evidence found it: Stolt-Nielsen's 166-vessel chemical-tanker fleet publicly rerouted via Suez in Nov 2023 (TradeWinds/Bloomberg/AJOT/SupplyChainBrain), and Maersk used a Balboa-Manzanillo rail land bridge to bypass the canal for part of its OC1 service (CNBC/gCaptain) — both now recorded in the 2023-2024 event's 'routing' field above. No source found gives a total-fleet diversion percentage, so this remains real but likely modest in scale relative to the much larger population that queued or paid auction premiums instead rather than physically diverting.
